string-array.item: For nowhere either with more quiet or more freedom from trouble does a man retire than into his own soul.\n— Marcus Aurelius, Meditations IV.3
Occupy thyself with few things, says the philosopher, if thou wouldst be tranquil.\n— Marcus Aurelius, Meditations IV.24
If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs thee, but thy own judgement about it.\n— Marcus Aurelius, Meditations VIII.47

Let not future things disturb thee, for thou wilt come to them, if it shall be necessary, having with thee the same reason which now thou usest for present things.\n— Marcus Aurelius, Meditations VII.8
Such as are thy habitual thoughts, such also will be the character of thy mind; for the soul is dyed by the thoughts.\n— Marcus Aurelius, Meditations V.16
Look within. Within is the fountain of good, and it will ever bubble up, if thou wilt ever dig.\n— Marcus Aurelius, Meditations VII.59
The present is the only thing of which a man can be deprived, if it is true that this is the only thing which he has.\n— Marcus Aurelius, Meditations II.14
Claim yourself for yourself.\n— after Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 1
While we put things off, life runs past.\n— after Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 1
The first sign of a settled mind is that it can stay in one place and linger with itself.\n— after Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 2
Whoever is everywhere is nowhere.\n— after Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 2
We suffer more often in imagination than in reality.\n— after Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 13
It is your mind you need to change, not the sky above you.\n— after Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 28
What good is silence all around if the feelings within are roaring?\n— after Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 56
Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things.\n— Epictetus, Enchiridion 5
Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.\n— Epictetus, Enchiridion 8
Of things some are in our power, and others are not.\n— Epictetus, Enchiridion 1
Who can make the muddy water clear? Let it be still, and it will gradually become clear.\n— Laozi, Tao Te Ching 15
The journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.\n— Laozi, Tao Te Ching 64
Thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty space that the use of the wheel depends.\n— Laozi, Tao Te Ching 11
The five colours blind the eye; the five notes deafen the ear.\n— after Laozi, Tao Te Ching 12
Who knows when to stop is free from danger.\n— after Laozi, Tao Te Ching 44
He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent.\n— Laozi, Tao Te Ching 33
The old pond. A frog jumps in, the sound of water.\n— after Bashō (1686)
Stillness. The cicadas\' voices seep into the rocks.\n— after Bashō, The Narrow Road to the Deep North
The thief left it behind: the moon in the window.\n— after Ryōkan
Sitting quietly, doing nothing, spring comes, and the grass grows by itself.\n— after the Zenrin kushū
Put on your clothes, eat your meal, and when you are tired, lie down.\n— after Linji (Record of Linji)
When I dance, I dance; when I sleep, I sleep.\n— after Montaigne, Essays III.13
All of our unhappiness comes from one thing: not knowing how to stay quietly in a room.\n— after Pascal, Pensées 139
Our life is frittered away by detail. … Simplify, simplify.\n— Thoreau, Walden
Time is but the stream I go a-fishing in.\n— Thoreau, Walden
Be patient toward all that is unsolved in your heart, and try to love the questions themselves.\n— after Rilke, Letters to a Young Poet
